QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Al-Qurtubi prefers aw in its ordinary sense, with ellipsis: illness preventing water use, or travel with no water and a need for it. BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 (author): The illness may make water use dangerous or prevent reaching it; in either case, the person is treated as lacking water. NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 (author): The dry-ablution command covers the sick, travelers, people with minor impurity, and those in major impurity; it applies when each lacks usable water for the relevant reason. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (author): Not finding water normally means searching without reaching it; for the sick, existing water that cannot be used counts legally as absent. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (الزمخشري): Al-Zamakhsharī explains that illness and travel are named first because they commonly create need for the concession, then the rule extends to anyone obliged to purify but lacking water through an enemy, beast, missing drawing tool, isolation, or similar cause. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (بعض العلماء): Some scholars permit tayammum for illness generally, relying on the verse’s broad wording. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (author): The verse guards prayer from impairment by drunkenness, junub status, or minor impurity, while making a merciful tayammum exception for illness or lack of water. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (مجاهد): Mujahid says a sick person who becomes junub and fears for his life receives the same tayammum concession as a traveler without water. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (author): The wording's general expression followed by detail is more eloquent and emphatic than explicitly listing travelers and patients lacking water, while accommodating different levels of understanding. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (author): Illness means any condition that prevents water use, whether because water cannot be reached or cannot safely be used. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (قيل): Travel is mentioned to connect illness with travel and equate them through inability to use water, even when water is present. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (بعضهم): A proposal reorders the verse: prohibit prayer in intoxication, janaba, or after either event, then command tayammum for illness or travel; al-Alusi objects that it splits condition and result without rationale. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (author): Al-Alusi prefers the apparent order: waterlessness can mean inability to use water and govern all cases, or retain its literal sense without attaching it to illness and travel. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (author): Illness and travel need not be restricted to people already in minor or major impurity: the verse explains the switch from water purification to tayammum. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (author): People outside illness and travel illustrate that inability to use water for other reasons also licenses tayammum; the ritual event itself is not the cause. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (قيل): One explanation says water absence also conditions illness and travel, but need not be repeated because major impurity is already clear there and minor impurity follows by textual implication. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (مالك): In the Baghdadi transmission, a patient unable to use water may perform multiple prayers with one tayammum until a nullifier; this also applies to missed prayers, and no Malik report addresses a junub person who then loses wudu. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (author): The water condition does not restrict the sick person's tayammum, because the meaning of illness already indicates the concession. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (author): The sick person is not merely someone chronically bedridden, since someone can usually bring water to such a person. ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 (author): When water is unavailable or cannot be used due to illness, tayammum replaces both the full bath after intercourse and the partial pre-prayer ablution. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): Illness or travel alone does not grant the tayammum dispensation; water must also be unavailable or unusable. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): Because residents and healthy people may also perform tayammum when water is absent, the commentary asks why illness and travel are singled out. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): Another answer is that illness and travel are singled out because water is more likely to be absent or unusable then. {"id": "4:43/q15", "question": "What journeys qualify for tayammum?", "turns_on": "The cited interpretations, reports, language arguments, and legal evidence differ.", "positions": [{"id": "4:43/q15/p1", "position": "Travel when water is unavailable", "reasons": "IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 (فرقة): Another group disallows tayammum during sinful travel; Ibn ʿAṭiyya also judges this weak. IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 (author): A traveler may lack water because none exists, searching risks missing companions, baggage is endangered, or predators or other harm threaten. TABRISI, d. 548 (علي وابن عباس وسعيد بن جبير ومجاهد): One interpretation forbids prayer in janaba except for travelers, who may pray using tayammum even though it does not remove janaba. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (أصحاب الشافعي): They argue the travel and water ruling follows as a separate rule: readers prefer pausing at ‘until you wash,’ so the earlier exception should not depend on the later verse’s condition. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): A traveler who lacks water must use tayammum whether the journey is long or short. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Scholars agree tayammum is allowed while travelling, but disagree about residence: Malik, his followers, Abu Hanifa, and Muhammad allow it there too. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن عمر): Ibn Umar reportedly would not leave his travel route to seek water even when it lay two bowshots away; Ishaq says one need search only where one is. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): A traveler may tayammum if water is entirely or partly unavailable, or seeking it risks losing companions or baggage, encountering thieves or beasts, missing prayer time, or causing thirst to oneself or another; cooking necessary food also counts. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو سعيد الخدري): In the report of Abu Said, two travelers pray after tayammum; the Prophet says the one who does not repeat followed the Sunna and the one who repeats earns double reward. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو داود): Abu Dawud transmits the two-traveler report and notes that the Abu Said link is not preserved in other narrations; al-Daraqutni's version specifies finding water within the prayer time. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (قتادة): Asked about travel tayammum, Qatada reports Ibn Umar’s elbow limit; al-Hasan and Ibrahim al-Nakha‘i also held it. BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 (author): The traveler is excused when water is unavailable. BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 (author): The exception attaches to “while junub,” exempting travel when water is unavailable and tayammum is used, as the following clause indicates. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (أبو حنيفة): Abū Ḥanīfa allows tayammum for someone who leaves town without intending travel if water is a mile away; another view sets the distance where people's voices cannot be heard. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (author): Travel permits tayammum whether the journey is long or short. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (عمار بن ياسر): Ammar ibn Yasir reports that after he became junub while traveling and rolled in dust, the Prophet taught him that tayammum requires only striking the earth and wiping the face and palms. SUYUTI-LUBAB, d. 911 (علي): ʿAlī says the clause about being ritually impure except when passing through concerns a traveler who became impure, performed dry ablution, and prayed. BURSEVI, d. 1127 (author): A traveler excused by travel may pray using dry ablution while junub; the prohibition lasts until washing. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (الهداية): Al-Hidaya allows tayammum for someone without water who is traveling or at least a mile outside town. ELMALILI, d. 1361 (author): Abirin sabil means people traveling on the road or in a state of travel; the exception concerns tayammum. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (author): The failure to find water is attached to the conditional clause and limits the traveler, one coming from the privy, and one touching women. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): Although the verse later explicitly refers to travelers, this interpretation says the phrase is repeated because water is less available or more needed during travel. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): Scholars agree tayammum is permissible during travel when water is absent or an obstacle prevents its use. {"id": "4:43/q19", "question": "What does touching women mean?", "turns_on": "The cited interpretations, reports, language arguments, and legal evidence differ.", "positions": [{"id": "4:43/q19/p1", "position": "Both bodily contact and intercourse", "reasons": "TABRISI, d. 548 (ابن عباس): When Arabs and non-Arabs disagreed whether it meant intercourse or touching, Ibn Abbas said the non-Arabs were right: it means intercourse, called touch because it leads to intercourse. TABRISI, d. 548 (علي وابن عباس ومجاهد والسدي وقتادة): One interpretation takes touching women to mean intercourse; Abu Hanifa and al-Jubbaʾi adopt it. IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 (علي، ابن عباس، الحسن، مجاهد، قتادة): One legal interpretation takes touching women to mean sexual intercourse. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (أنصار قول الجماع): Supporters of the intercourse interpretation cite Qur’anic euphemisms for intercourse at 2:37 and 58:3; Ibn ʿAbbās says God is modest and noble, veiling the meaning with ‘touching.’ | mentions 2:37, 58:3 RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (أنصار قول الجماع): They also argue that ‘coming from the place of need’ already covers minor impurity; if touching women also meant minor impurity, the verse would omit major impurity, so it must mean intercourse. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): The three reported meanings are intercourse, physical contact, or a word covering both; most readers treat the two readings as equivalent in sense. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (محمد بن يزيد): Muhammad b. Yazid says lamastum more naturally means kissing or the like, since each party acts; lamistum means intercourse or touching, where the woman does not act. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن العربي): Ibn al-ʿArabi says the verse assigns three clauses to three rulings: janaba, minor impurity, and touch or kissing; treating touch as intercourse would repeat the meaning. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Although the reciprocal form mulamasa is said to require two actors, al-Qurtubi answers that both parties can be described as toucher and touched; Arabic also uses reciprocal verbs for one actor. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Masḥ can mean intercourse, cutting with a sword, a camel's day's travel, a woman without buttocks, or a touch of beauty; here it means dragging the hand across the object. NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 (علي وابن عباس): Ali and Ibn ʿAbbās explain touching women here as sexual intercourse. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (author): The long-alif form can correspond to the simple verb, like جاوزت الشيء وجزته; its form does not distinguish active from passive though the meaning can, and al-Shāfiʿī applies it to both toucher and touched in his stronger view. SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 (غير مسمى): One interpretation makes فاعل equivalent to a simple verb; another says لمس means intercourse while لامس denotes touching short of intercourse. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (ابن عمر وعبيدة وأبو عثمان النهدي وأبو عبيدة وعامر الشعبي وثابت بن الحجاج وإبراهيم النخعي وزيد بن أسلم): Ibn Abi Hatim transmits the interpretation that touch means less than intercourse from these authorities as well. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (ناصر هذه المقالة): Advocates of the physical-touch reading cite Quran 6:7, prophetic usage toward Ma‘iz, the hadith about the hand’s zina, Aisha’s report of the Prophet kissing and touching his wives, and the Sahihayn prohibition of touch-sale; they say Arabic uses the word for both touch and intercourse. | mentions 6:7 IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (ابن عباس وعلي وأبي بن كعب ومجاهد وطاوس والحسن وعبيد بن عمير وسعيد بن جبير والشعبي وقتادة ومقاتل بن حيان): One interpretation takes touching women as a euphemism for intercourse, held by these authorities; Quranic uses of touching in divorce contexts support that sense. | mentions 2:237, 33:49 BURHAN, d. 794 (author): The Qur'an euphemizes intercourse with terms for touching, intimacy, marital union, entry, and covering, drawing on bodily contact and clothing or cultivation metaphors. BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 (الشافعي): Al-Shāfiʿī allows lamastum to mean literal skin contact, intercourse caused by contact, or a particular kind of touching; intercourse can be named by its cause or the whole by a part. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (علي بن أبي طالب): Ali says “touching women” means sexual intercourse, expressed euphemistically by God. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas glosses touching women as sexual intercourse. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (ابن عباس): In a discussion, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Ata, and the non-Arab clients argued for hand-touch, while Ubayd ibn Umayr and the Arabs argued for intercourse; Ibn Abbas judged the Arabs right, since touch-related terms can euphemize intercourse. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas tells Nafi ibn al-Azraq that the verse means intercourse, though Hudhayl uses the word for hand-touch; he cites Labid and al-Aʿsha's poems as evidence for that Arabic usage. ITQAN, d. 911 (author): The reported difference over whether لامستم means intercourse or touching by hand is no disagreement: intercourse fits لامستم, and hand-touch fits لمستم. BURSEVI, d. 1127 (author): Touching women here means having intercourse with them. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (author): “Touching women” euphemistically means intercourse, indicating major impurity, while the preceding clause indicates minor impurity. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (ابن مسعود والنخعي والشعبي): Ibn Masʿud, al-Nakhaʿi, and al-Shaʿbi interpret the phrase as skin touching short of intercourse. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (بعضهم): Others prefer interpreting both readings as intercourse, privileging figurative usage and reconciling the readings; this matches the Hanafi position. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (author): Touch literally means bodily contact, and metaphorically can mean seeking or finding, descending, or sexual intercourse; the cited poem witnesses the sense of descending, while 2:237 uses it for intercourse. | mentions 72:8, 2:237 KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): Lems and mulamasa literally mean touching with a hand or part of the body, while figuratively they mean sexual intercourse.
